cret-105.title: A disputed anoxic event in the Coniacian–Santonian
cret-105.text: Not every black shale tells a global story. A minor oceanic anoxic event, recorded by organic-rich black shales, has been proposed for the Coniacian–Santonian, about 89.8–83.6 million years ago. An anoxic event is a time when large expanses of ocean lost their dissolved oxygen, leaving waters both anoxic and sulfidic, and so toxic. Such events can be read as the Earth's response to excess carbon dioxide injected into air and water. These shales are more local than those of the major Cretaceous events, found mainly in the Atlantic and nearby areas. Some researchers therefore tie them to local conditions rather than to global change.

cret-109.title: The first duck-billed hadrosaurids
cret-109.text: The duck-billed dinosaurs would become some of the most common plant-eaters of the latest Cretaceous. Their family, the hadrosaurids, first appears around 86 million years ago. They descended from Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous iguanodonts and kept a similar body layout. Their teeth were different: stacked into complex dental batteries that made effective grinding surfaces, unlike those of more primitive iguanodonts. They could also switch stance. In some species the young walked mostly on two legs and the adults mostly on four. Its members included nest-builders like {{ref:cret-108}}.

cret-111.title: The Praia Grande crater, hidden off Brazil
cret-111.text: Off the coast of Brazil, a scar from space lies under 4 km of rock. An impact in the Santonian made the Praia Grande crater, about 20 km across, in the Santos Basin. The basin lies about 200 kilometres southeast of the São Paulo State coastline. Buried deep beneath younger sediment, the crater is well preserved. It counts only as a possible impact crater: Petrobras identified it on 3D seismic data in 2004.

cret-113.title: The High Arctic volcanoes flare again
cret-113.text: Some volcanic provinces erupt for tens of millions of years. The High Arctic Large Igneous Province was active from about 130 to 60 million years ago. About 85 million years ago it entered a second phase. From then until about 60 million years ago, it poured out mildly alkaline flood basalts, with a geochemical makeup similar to intra-plate composition. The flood basalts in the Canadian Arctic Islands resemble the Columbia River flood basalts of the Pacific Northwest of the United States.

cret-119.title: The Ninety East Ridge, a 5,000 km volcanic trail
cret-119.text: A single hotspot built a ridge as long as a country. The Kerguelen hotspot raised the 5,000 km Ninety East Ridge between 82 and 38 million years ago, at or near a spreading ridge. Around 60 million years ago, in the late Paleocene, parts of it stood above water for 2–3 million years as volcanic islands, probably 1,000 km from the nearest land. Yet the ridge shows no systematic isotopic variation. That is inconsistent with an ageing mantle plume for all of it, which suggests at least two hotspots contributed. The area also lies on the diffuse boundary between the Indian and Australian plates.

cret-120.title: The oldest Hawaiian–Emperor volcanoes
cret-120.text: Hawaii is the young end of a very old chain. The oldest dated volcano of the Hawaiian hotspot chain, at its northern end, is 81 million years old. The Emperor seamounts, the chain's oldest and most eroded part, are 39 to 85 million years old. The fifteen volcanoes of the eight principal Hawaiian islands are the youngest of more than 129 volcanoes stretching 5,800 kilometers across the North Pacific. In 1963 John Tuzo Wilson hypothesized that an essentially stationary hotspot made the chain as the Pacific plate drifted northwest, leaving a trail of increasingly eroded islands and seamounts.

cret-121.title: The first palm trees
cret-121.text: Palms arrived in the fossil record around 80 million years ago, by the date used here. Yet the family, Arecaceae, was the first modern family of monocots to appear, around 108 million years ago in the Early Cretaceous. That is earlier than the date given for this entry.

cret-124.title: Lappajärvi, a Finnish lake in an impact crater
cret-124.text: A rock about 1.6 km across left one of Finland's largest lakes. An asteroid of that size struck about 77.85 million years ago, in the Campanian. It left a crater about 22–23 km wide and 750 m deep, now Lake Lappajärvi. In 2001 uranium-lead dating by the Geological Survey of Finland put the crater's age at around 73.3 million years, give or take five million. Other dating methods give different ages, so the exact date is not settled.

cret-128.title: The first Velociraptor
cret-128.text: The famous raptor was smaller than most people expect. Velociraptor first appears around 75 million years ago and lived in Asia until about 71 million years ago. It was a small dromaeosaurid, about 1.5–2.07 m long, with a body mass of around 14.1–19.7 kg, smaller than Deinonychus and Achillobator. Its long, low skull with an upturned snout sets it apart from other dromaeosaurids.

cret-129.title: The Manson impact in Iowa
cret-129.text: Under the flat fields of Iowa lies one of North America's largest known impact scars. An asteroid or comet nucleus struck near present-day Manson about 74 million years ago, leaving a buried structure about 35 km across. Nothing shows at the surface, because comparatively recent glacial till covers it and the site is now a flat landscape. Some dating of the core gives a different age, so sources do not agree exactly.

cret-131.title: The last Bennettitales
cret-131.text: Once among the most common seed plants of the Mesozoic, the Bennettitales ended as a polar remnant. These shrubs and cycad-like plants, also called cycadeoids, had been present since the Permian. They were widespread in the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, then declined severely in the Late Cretaceous as flowering plants rose. They died out in most areas toward the end of the Cretaceous, with the last northern records in polar latitudes. Where they belong among seed plants remains uncertain.

cret-133.title: The Maastrichtian sea-level fall
cret-133.text: The sea itself retreated as the Cretaceous ended. Sea level fell in the final stage by more than at any other time in the Mesozoic. This Maastrichtian regression is one of the proposed contributors to the K–Pg extinction. A massive fall would have greatly shrunk the continental shelf margin, which could have caused a mass extinction for marine species only. Some argue it was the most likely cause because the boundary layers show no distortion or tilting related to mountains. The case is contradicted by sections that show no sign of marine regression yet still show a major drop in diversity.

cret-138.title: Mosasaurus, the last giant sea lizard
cret-138.text: Mosasaurus evolves around 70 million years ago, and it was not alone. In the Maastrichtian, several large mosasaurs shared and competed in the Tethys Sea. Mosasaurus faced other large predatory mosasaurs such as Prognathodon and Tylosaurus, which fed on similar prey. They coexisted through niche partitioning. Another source gives Mosasaurus a longer range, about 82 to 66 million years ago, across the Campanian and Maastrichtian.

cret-139.title: Multituberculates, rodents before rodents
cret-139.text: The most successful of the early mammals were gnawers. Multituberculates increased in diversity around 70 million years ago. They were the most diverse order of Mesozoic mammals, with more than 200 species ranging from mouse-sized to beaver-sized. By the Cenomanian, early in the Late Cretaceous, the Cimolodonta had replaced all other multituberculate lineages. In the Late Cretaceous they radiated as herbivores and into forms like squirrel-like tree dwellers, peaking in diversity.

cret-140.title: The Labrador Sea begins to open
cret-140.text: The Labrador Sea started opening 69 million years ago, in the Maastrichtian. Seafloor spreading in its southern part moved Greenland north relative to North America. Sources disagree on the timing. One says the sea formed as the North American and Greenland plates separated, starting about 60 million years ago in the Paleocene and stopping about 40 million years ago. Spreading in Baffin Bay and the Labrador Sea slowed, became oblique, and ceased between 45 and 36 million years ago. The cited 1989 paper dates the initial opening to 92 Ma, not the 69 Ma used here.

cret-143.title: Quetzalcoatlus, a giant of the skies
cret-143.text: Few animals ever matched it for size in the air. Quetzalcoatlus first appears around 68 million years ago. Its type specimen, found in 1971 in the Javelina Formation of Texas, is just several wing fragments, and it was described as Quetzalcoatlus northropi in 1975. That species is a candidate for the largest flying animal ever found, though its size is hard to estimate from a fragmentary specimen. Azhdarchids like it were highly terrestrial by pterosaur standards, yet even the largest could fly.

cret-150.title: The last belemnites
cret-150.text: Belemnites were already declining and confined to a few high-latitude regions when they died out in the K–Pg extinction. Like ammonites, their embryos probably could not survive ocean acidification, and sea butterflies replaced their larvae in the food chain. The loss mattered: belemnites had been an important food source for many Mesozoic marine creatures, both adults and planktonic juveniles.

cret-152.title: The last pterosaurs
cret-152.text: No pterosaur survived the K–Pg extinction. Azhdarchid and nyctosaurid pterosaurs were present in the Maastrichtian and likely died out at the boundary. Pterosaurs were an extinct clade of warm-blooded flying reptiles. They were not dinosaurs, which are defined as descendants of the last common ancestor of Saurischia and Ornithischia.

cret-155.title: Shiva, a disputed second crater
cret-155.text: A crater far larger than Chicxulub would be hard to miss, and that is the claim. The potential Shiva crater, 450–600 km across, has been dated to about 66 million years ago. It is a proposed impact crater on the Indian continental shelf, offshore west of Mumbai. Sankar Chatterjee and colleagues proposed that it formed at the K–Pg boundary and helped cause the extinction. He suggested that Shiva, Chicxulub and other possible craters came from multiple impacts. Shiva remains only a proposed, unconfirmed structure.

pale-024.title: The Deccan fires die down
pale-024.text: Most of the Deccan lava came out in a flash of geological time. The bulk erupted from fissures in the Western Ghats between 66 and 65 Ma, and two-thirds may have formed within a million years around 65.5 Ma. India's plate motion slowed around 63 Ma, by which time the main phase had ended. The Deccan Traps may originally have covered about 1.5 million km2, with a correspondingly larger volume. Erosion and plate tectonics reduced them, and the lava flows directly observable now cover around 500,000 km2.

pale-033.title: Eritherium, an elephant ancestor the size of a cat
pale-033.text: The ancestor of the elephants weighed about as much as a house cat. Proboscideans, the elephant order, first evolved in Africa around 60 Ma, during the Selandian. The earliest known, Eritherium, weighed only about 3–8 kg. Later proboscideans are distinguished by enormous size, tusks and long muscular trunks, which were less developed or absent in the early ones. By the Early Eocene, proboscideans began growing in size.

eoce-010.title: Gastornis, the giant flightless bird
eoce-010.text: A bird taller than most of its neighbors could not fly. Gastornis, a large flightless bird, appears in the fossil record about 56 million years ago and went extinct about 40 million years ago. No fossil of it has been found younger than about 45 million years. Its relatives are still debated: a 2024 study found little support for Gastornithiformes and placed Gastornis in the Galliformes crown group, closer to Phasianoidea than to megapodes.

eoce-020.title: The London Clay's tropical flora
eoce-020.text: Palm-like fruits from southeast England look like a tropical market. Shallow seas over the region laid down the London Clay, rich in fossil seeds and fruits of some 350 plant species. Its flora includes tropical plants now found in Asia, reflecting the much warmer early Eocene climate. Collectors have gathered these plant fossils for almost 300 years. The clay itself is stiff and bluish, turning brown when weathered and oxidized.

eoce-025.title: Eocene Thermal Maximum 3
eoce-025.text: ETM-3, informally the K or X event, was another early Eocene hyperthermal, a brief warm spike marked by a pulse of isotopically light carbon. Its carbon-isotope excursion marks the onset of the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. Sources differ on the date. Another gives about 52.5 million years ago, after ETM2 at about 53.2 million years ago.

eoce-026.title: Cambay amber, an Indian insect trap
eoce-026.text: Insects trapped in resin in Gujarat give a glimpse of a world in motion. The Cambay amber preserves an important early Eocene assemblage of arthropods, mainly insects, and mayflies have been found in it. It was being deposited at the peak of the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. India was colliding with Asia then, acting as a biotic ferry, so the amber may help show the biotic interchange between the two landmasses.

eoce-035.title: The Sevier orogeny ends
eoce-035.text: A mountain-building episode that began about 160 million years ago finally stopped. Deformation in the Sevier fold-and-thrust belt of western North America ended around 50 Ma, though in southwestern Utah some thrusts may have stayed active until later in the Eocene. The orogeny affected western North America from northern Canada to Mexico. It was preceded by the Nevadan, Sonoman and Antler orogenies and partially overlapped in time and space with the Laramide orogeny.

eoce-034.title: Monte Bolca, the fishbowl of Verona
eoce-034.text: Near Verona, a lack of oxygen in the mud preserved fish almost as they lived. Their organs are often intact and skin colour can sometimes be read. The Pesciara ('fishbowl') is famous for extraordinarily well preserved Eocene fish. Monte Bolca is rich, with 250 species in 140 genera, 90 families and 19 orders. It has the most diverse fish fauna of any Cenozoic fossil site, with many of the earliest fossil occurrences of modern marine fish groups.

eoce-039.title: Rifts open across western Europe
eoce-039.text: A crack more than a thousand kilometers long opened across western Europe. The ongoing Alpine collision opened a north–south rift system from the Eocene onward. The European Cenozoic Rift System is 1,100 km long, formed in the foreland of the Alps as the lithosphere responded to the Alpine and Pyrenean orogenies. It began to form in the Late Eocene. The Limagne Graben formed in the middle Eocene, holding a lake, and rifting also began in the Bresse Graben. Parts, especially the Upper and Lower Rhine Grabens, remain seismically active and cause most of the larger earthquakes in Europe north of the Alps.

eoce-040.title: Grasses spread and the first savannas appear
eoce-040.text: Open grassland is a young idea. Grasses began to spread as the climate cooled and dried after the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, moving out from riverbanks into open tracts. Subhumid savannas are known in South America from the middle Eocene. The middle Eocene shifted to a cooler climate around 47.8 Ma, briefly interrupted by the Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum. The Eocene held the warmest period of the Cenozoic and also marked the decline into an icehouse climate and the rapid expansion of the Antarctic ice sheet. One timeline places the first grasslands later, around 35 Ma.

eoce-044.title: The Kula plate disappears beneath Alaska
eoce-044.text: An entire ocean plate vanished under Alaska. The Kula plate, subducting under Alaska and the Yukon since the early Eocene, was entirely consumed around 48 million years ago. Only a slab in the mantle under the Bering Sea remains. Another source says nearly all of it had been subducted beneath the North American Plate by about 40 million years ago, and that Kula–Pacific spreading ceased then as the Kula plate joined the Pacific plate.

eoce-043.title: Geiseltal, a German lignite treasure
eoce-043.text: A coastal moorland of lakes and tidal bays in central Germany preserved over 50,000 fossil vertebrates, plus insects and plants. The Geiseltal fossils, especially the vertebrates and mammals, are uniquely preserved in lignite, found nowhere else in Central Europe. Soft tissues were among the very first found from the Eocene, and the mammals define a European land-mammal stage. The lignite is divided into four main seams, of which the lower three were mainly fossil-bearing.

eoce-050.title: Kishenehn's blood-filled mosquito
eoce-050.text: A mosquito that had just fed lies in Montana stone. Oil shale of the Kishenehn Formation, a Paleogene stratigraphic unit, preserves exquisitely detailed insects. These include a blood-filled mosquito with traces of hemoglobin.

eoce-056.title: The Quercy 'natural mummies'
eoce-056.text: Fissures in southern France became natural tombs. These karst deposits hold mammals, birds, turtles, crocodiles, plants and insects. Some amphibians and lizards are preserved as articulated 'natural mummies' with soft tissue. Nearly all fly pupae were preserved as isolated endocasts, many still covered by the puparium, the hardened skin of the last larval instar. The first phosphate deposits in Quercy were discovered in 1869 and published independently by Daubré and Trutat in 1871.

eoce-058.title: India and Australia fuse into one plate
eoce-058.text: Two plates became one. The Indo-Australian plate formed when the Indian and Australian plates fused, approximately 43 million years ago, after the mid-ocean ridge between them ceased spreading. The union is not perfect. Along the northern Ninety East Ridge there appears to be a weakness zone where the two plates are going different ways. Differential movement has compressed the plate near its centre at Sumatra, with a possible division into separate Indian and Australian plates again.

eoce-059.title: The Logoisk crater in Belarus
eoce-059.text: Drillers looking for something else found a buried crater. A meteorite struck near Lahoysk, Belarus, about 42.3 million years ago, leaving a 15 km crater, now buried. It was found by accident during routine exploration drilling near the village of Kuzevichi in the 1970s. Drilling found Quaternary deposits to 160 m, then 230 m of layered clays and lacustrine sediments, then 240 m of breccias. It was suggested that the crater may contain impact diamonds, but this has not been confirmed.

eoce-060.title: A burst of magnetic reversals
eoce-060.text: The magnetic field can get restless. Around 42 million years ago, Earth's field flipped 17 times in 3 million years. Earlier, in a 4-million-year window centred on 54 Ma, there were 10 reversals. There have been at least 183 reversals over the last 83 million years, on average once every 450,000 years or so. The rate has varied widely over time.

eoce-065.title: The Eridanos, a lost Baltic river
eoce-065.text: A river that no longer exists once drained much of northern Europe. The Eridanos began to form about 40 million years ago and flowed through what is now the Baltic Sea. Its remnants are found from the North Sea and the Netherlands in the west to sediments in northern Lapland. Neogene uplift of the South Swedish Dome deflected it from its path across south-central Sweden to a course south of Sweden in the Pliocene. After it disappeared, the Rhine became the most important river in this part of the North Sea Basin.

eoce-070.title: Rifting begins in northern Kenya
eoce-070.text: Africa began to split in the north. Volcanism and rifting began around Turkana in northern Kenya 40–35 million years ago, then spread north and south along the Gregory Rift. When rifting reached the Tanzanian Craton, the rift divided into the eastern Gregory Rift and the western Albertine Rift, separated by the 1,300 kilometres wide East African Plateau. The rift is widest at its northern end in the Afar region, narrowing to a few kilometers in northern Tanzania.
